table.caption: Annual mean CO₂ at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, in parts per million (NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory)

options: CO₂ measured at Mauna Loa since 1958
A graph of ozone over Antarctica
A dose-response curve for carbon dioxide
A map of global surface temperatures

why.correct: The Keeling curve is the continuous record of atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, begun in 1958.
options: Right: Charles David Keeling began the measurements in Hawaii in 1958.
Ozone records are a different data set.
It is a record of CO₂ in the air over time, not a toxicity curve.
It tracks CO₂ concentration, not temperature.

items.q: How do scientists know how much CO₂ was in the air 10,000 years ago?
options: Measurements at Mauna Loa
Air bubbles trapped in ice cores
Counting tree rings in living trees
Satellite images of the ozone layer

why.correct: Snow that turns to ice traps tiny bubbles of air; drilling ice cores in Antarctica and Greenland samples air hundreds of thousands of years old.
options: Mauna Loa measurements began in 1958.
Right: bubbles in old ice hold samples of past air.
Tree rings show past growth and climate, not air samples.
Satellites began in the 20th century and image ozone, not ancient air.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in CO₂ at Mauna Loa from 1960 to 2020, then the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the old value, the 1960 level (316.91 ppm), not the 2020 level.
Multiply by 100 to turn the fraction into a percent.
97.3 is the change in ppm. Divide it by the 1960 value and multiply by 100 for a percent.

items.q: What was the average rate of increase in CO₂ from 2000 to 2020, in ppm per year?

mistakes.why: 44.5 ppm is the total rise over 20 years. Divide by 20 years for the rate per year.
Divide by the number of years, 2020 − 2000 = 20, not by 2.

items.q: How did the yearly rise in CO₂ in the 1960s compare with the 2010s?
options: Slower: about 0.9 then and 2.4 ppm a year now
It was faster: CO₂ rose most quickly in the 1960s
It was the same: about 2 ppm a year in both
CO₂ fell in the 1960s and rose in the 2010s

why.correct: The curve is not just rising; it is getting steeper, because yearly emissions have grown.
options: The 1960s rise was the smallest per decade in the table.
The 1960s rate was under 1 ppm a year.
CO₂ rose in every period in the table.

items.q: Which conclusion do the data best support?
options: CO₂ rose because the ozone hole grew
CO₂ rose each period, faster over time
CO₂ will level off before 2030
CO₂ in 2023 was about twice the 1960 value

why.correct: Describe trends with numbers: about 317 ppm in 1960 to 421 ppm in 2023, rising faster each decade.
options: The ozone hole does not add CO₂ to the air.
Right: every value is higher than the last, and each decade’s rise is larger.
The data show no sign of leveling off.
421.08 is about 1.33 times 316.91, not twice.

items.q: The Mauna Loa record also shows CO₂ rising and falling by a few ppm every year. What causes this yearly cycle?
options: Factories shut down for the summer each year
The ozone hole opens each spring
Northern plants grow in summer, using CO₂
Volcanoes in Hawaii erupt each winter

why.correct: Photosynthesis in the Northern Hemisphere summer draws CO₂ down; decomposition and respiration in winter release it.
options: Emissions are fairly steady through the year.
The ozone hole does not change CO₂.
Right: most land and plants are in the Northern Hemisphere, so their growing season sets the cycle.
Measurements are made to avoid volcanic air, and eruptions are not yearly.

items.q: Which human activity releases the most carbon dioxide?
options: Raising cattle
Using fertilizer on fields
Using spray cans
Burning fossil fuels

why.correct: Burning fossil fuels for electricity, transport, industry and heat releases most human CO₂; deforestation is the next largest.
options: Cattle are a major methane source.
Fertilizer is the main source of nitrous oxide.
Spray cans once released CFCs, not much CO₂.
Right: coal, oil and natural gas burned for energy are the largest source.

items.q: Which are major human sources of methane? Select all that apply.
options: Cattle and other livestock
Rice paddies
Landfills
Wind turbines
Solar panels
Catalytic converters

why.correct: Methane forms where organic matter breaks down without oxygen: livestock guts, flooded rice fields, landfills and leaking natural gas systems.
options: Right: microbes in cattle digestive systems make methane.
Right: flooded fields lack oxygen, so microbes make methane.
Right: buried waste decomposes without oxygen, making methane.
Wind turbines do not release methane while running.
Solar panels do not release methane while running.
Catalytic converters reduce car pollutants; they are not a methane source.

items.q: Which is the largest human source of nitrous oxide?
options: Burning coal in power plants
Nitrogen fertilizer on soils
Leaks from natural gas pipelines
Clearcutting tropical forests

why.correct: Agriculture, mainly nitrogen fertilizer and manure, is the largest human source of nitrous oxide.
options: Coal releases mostly CO₂ and SO₂; it is a smaller N₂O source.
Right: soil microbes turn some of the added nitrogen into N₂O.
Pipelines leak methane.
Clearcutting releases mostly CO₂.

items.q: Ice cores show CO₂ stayed between about 180 and 300 ppm for 800,000 years. What does today’s value of over 420 ppm suggest?
options: CO₂ is in the middle of its natural range
Ice cores are probably measured wrongly
CO₂ is far above its natural range
CO₂ has fallen since the last ice age

why.correct: Natural cycles moved CO₂ between about 180 ppm (ice ages) and 300 ppm (warm periods); human emissions pushed it beyond 420 ppm.
options: Over 420 ppm is well above 300 ppm.
Ice core and direct measurements agree where they overlap.
Right: today’s level is well outside the 800,000-year range.
CO₂ has risen, not fallen.

items.q: Before about 1800, CO₂ was about 280 ppm. In 2023 the Mauna Loa annual mean was 421.08 ppm. By what percent has CO₂ risen?

mistakes.why: You divided by the new value. Use (new − old) ÷ old × 100: (421.08 − 280) ÷ 280 × 100.

items.q: Clearing a tropical forest by burning adds CO₂ to the air in two ways. What are they?
options: It releases stored carbon and removes a sink
Burning makes ozone, and ozone turns into CO₂
Ash releases CFCs, and CFCs make CO₂
Smoke blocks sunlight, and soil releases more nitrogen

why.correct: Trees store carbon. Burning releases it, and losing the forest removes a carbon sink.
options: Right: the forest goes from a carbon sink to a source.
Ozone does not turn into CO₂.
Ash does not release CFCs.
This does not describe the two ways CO₂ increases.

items.q: Explain how burning coal for electricity raises the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere.

why.correct: Coal is ancient stored carbon. Burning moves it to the air faster than natural sinks can take it back.

specific.frame: Burning coal ___ carbon that was stored underground, which ___ CO₂ in the air faster than ___ can remove it.

verb.label: What burning does
options: releases
stores
destroys

why.1: Burning releases carbon; storing would remove it from the air.
why.2: Carbon is not destroyed; it combines with oxygen to form CO₂.

effect.label: Effect on CO₂
options: increases
decreases

why.1: Burning adds CO₂, so it increases.

sink.label: What cannot keep up
options: plants and the ocean
the ozone layer
acid rain

why.1: The ozone layer does not remove CO₂.
why.2: Acid rain does not remove CO₂ from the air.

specific.model: Burning coal releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years as CO₂, which increases CO₂ in the air faster than plants and the ocean can remove it, because these sinks absorb only part of each year’s emissions.

items.q: In the ice core record, what was the highest CO₂ level before the industrial era?
options: About 420 ppm
About 180 ppm
About 290 ppm
About 800 ppm

why.correct: The peaks of the record, during warm periods between ice ages, reach about 290 ppm.
options: That is today’s level, measured directly, not in the ice core record.
That is the lowest level, during ice ages.
Right: the highest peaks reach about 290 ppm.
800 is the number of thousands of years the record covers, not ppm.

items.q: What pattern does the record show over 800,000 years?
options: CO₂ rose steadily the whole time
CO₂ stayed at about 280 ppm the whole time
CO₂ fell steadily to today
CO₂ cycled between about 180 and 290 ppm

why.correct: Natural cycles, tied to ice ages, moved CO₂ up and down within a range.
options: It rose and fell many times.
It swung by about 100 ppm.
It cycled up and down.
Right: low in ice ages, high in warm periods, again and again.

items.q: How does today’s CO₂ level of over 420 ppm compare with the ice core record?
options: It is far above the highest natural peak
It is within the natural range
It is lower than in past warm periods
It matches the lowest point of the last ice age

why.correct: Human emissions have pushed CO₂ well beyond anything in the last 800,000 years.
options: Right: 420 ppm is about 130 ppm above the record’s highest peak.
The highest natural value was about 290 ppm.
Past warm periods reached about 290 ppm, far below 420.
Ice ages were near 180 ppm.
